message.content: {"passages":[{"reference":"6.11","text":"While Appion was interpreting these things allegorically, I was deep in thought and appeared not to be following what he was saying. So he broke off his discourse and said to me, “If you are not following what I am saying, why am I even having this discussion in the first place?” I replied, “Do not suppose that I am insensible to what you are saying, for I understand it very well, since this is not the first time I have heard it. To let you know that I am not ignorant of what you are saying, I will summarize what you have stated; and as for what you have omitted, I will complete the allegories in sequence, just as I heard them from others.” Appion said, “Do as you say.”","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"σύννους ὢν","chosen":"I was deep in thought","rationale":"σύννους describes being absorbed or pensive, which explains why Clement merely appeared not to be following."},{"source_quote":"τοῖς ὑπ’ αὐτοῦ λεγομένοις μὴ παρακολουθεῖν","chosen":"not to be following what he was saying","rationale":"παρακολουθέω here denotes following or comprehending the course of an argument."},{"source_quote":"τὰ μὲν σοι ῥηθέντα ἐπιτεμοῦμαι","chosen":"I will summarize what you have stated","rationale":"ἐπιτέμνομαι means to abridge or summarize; the dative σοι is understood as marking the speaker of the preceding statements."},{"source_quote":"τῶν δὲ παραλειφθέντων σοι κατ’ ἀκολουθίαν","chosen":"as for what you have omitted, I will complete the allegories in sequence","rationale":"κατ’ ἀκολουθίαν is taken as describing an orderly continuation; “by logical consequence” is also possible."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"6.12","text":"I now pass over giving a detailed account of the living egg brought forth from the chance blending of boundless matter. When it burst, according to some, a male-and-female being, Phanes, sprang out. I also summarize all those matters up to the point when the ruptured shell assumed its harmonious structure, while marrow-like matter from it remained; then, in outline, I run through the account of the things produced inwardly by that matter, together with what follows. For, as you say, from Cronus and Rhea—that is, by time and matter—were born first Pluto, as the sediment that settled below; second Poseidon, who is the middle, moist substance floating above the nature with the strongest downward pull; and third the highest substance, which is aether, namely Zeus. This third substance was not swallowed, but, being a hot force and having a nature that rises upward, it flew up, as if driven by some gust, into the most sovereign aether above.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ ἐκ τῆς ἀπείρου ὕλης κατὰ ἐπιτυχίαν κράσεως ἀποκυηθὲν ἔμψυχον ὠόν","chosen":"the living egg brought forth from the chance blending of boundless matter","rationale":"ἔμψυχον is rendered “living” rather than the more technical “ensouled”; κατὰ ἐπιτυχίαν presents the blending as occurring by chance."},{"source_quote":"ἀρρενόθηλυ ἐξέθορεν, Φάνης","chosen":"a male-and-female being, Phanes, sprang out","rationale":"The neuter compound ἀρρενόθηλυ denotes an androgynous or male-and-female entity, while ἐξέθορεν conveys a sudden springing forth."},{"source_quote":"τὸ ῥαγὲν κύτος τὴν ἁρμονίαν ἔλαβεν","chosen":"the ruptured shell assumed its harmonious structure","rationale":"κύτος can denote a hollow vessel, casing, or shell; τὴν ἁρμονίαν ἔλαβεν indicates acquiring an ordered or harmonious arrangement."},{"source_quote":"ἡ κάτω παραχωρήσασα ὑποστάθμη","chosen":"the sediment that settled below","rationale":"ὑποστάθμη denotes sediment or dregs, and παραχωρήσασα depicts it giving way or moving to the lower position."},{"source_quote":"τῇ κάτω ὀλκοτάτῃ φύσει","chosen":"the nature with the strongest downward pull","rationale":"The unusual ὀλκοτάτῃ is understood from the idea of drawing or pulling; κάτω specifies that the tendency is downward. “The lowest, most attractive nature” is a possible alternative."},{"source_quote":"εἰς τὸν ἄνω ἡγεμονικώτατον ἀνέπτη αἰθέρα","chosen":"it flew up into the most sovereign aether above","rationale":"ἡγεμονικώτατον characterizes the upper aether as ruling or preeminent; “most ruling” would be less idiomatic English."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"6.13","text":"Cronus’s bonds are the fastening together of heaven and earth, as I have also heard from others who give allegorical interpretations. The cutting off of his parts is the separation and differentiation of the elements, because all things were cut away from their own natural substance and set apart, each to be arranged by itself. Time no longer begets; instead, the things begotten through it carry on the succession by nature’s law. Aphrodite, who rose from the depth, is the generative substance arising from moisture. When the hot spirit mingles with it, it produces the desire for their union and brings the beauty of the world to completion.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"ἡ σύμπηξις οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς","chosen":"the fastening together of heaven and earth","rationale":"σύμπηξις denotes a joining, compacting, or solid fastening together."},{"source_quote":"ἡ δὲ ἀποκοπὴ τῶν μορίων","chosen":"the cutting off of his parts","rationale":"μορίων is the source’s euphemistic “parts”; the possessive “his” refers contextually to Cronus."},{"source_quote":"πάντα ἐκ τῆς ἰδίας φύσεως ἀπετμήθη","chosen":"all things were cut away from their own natural substance","rationale":"ἐκ is retained as marking source or separation. “Were divided according to their respective natures” is contextually possible but renders ἐκ less directly."},{"source_quote":"τὰ γεννηθέντα δι’ αὐτοῦ νόμῳ φύσεως ποιεῖται τὰς διαδοχάς","chosen":"the things begotten through it carry on the succession by nature’s law","rationale":"The neuter plural subject takes a singular verb; διαδοχάς may denote successive generations or succession more generally."},{"source_quote":"τὸν τῆς μίξεως ποιεῖται ἔρωτα","chosen":"it produces the desire for their union","rationale":"ἔρως can mean desire or erotic impulse, while τῆς μίξεως may describe either desire for the mixture or desire generated by it; the former fits the generative context."},{"source_quote":"τελεσιουργεῖ τοῦ κόσμου τὸ κάλλος","chosen":"brings the beauty of the world to completion","rationale":"τελεσιουργέω means to accomplish, perfect, or bring something fully into effect."}],"source_issues":[]},{"reference":"6.14","text":"The wedding banquet, where Zeus was holding the feast for the Nereid Thetis and the beautiful Peleus, has the following allegory—so that you may know, Appion, that we have heard such things even without you. The banquet, then, is the world; the twelve are the Fates’ heavenly encircling supports, which they call zodiacal signs; Prometheus is forethought, through which all things came to be; Peleus is mud, conceived from earth for the making of a human being and mixed with the Nereid—that is, with water. From the mixture of the two, water and earth, the first human was not begotten but molded, and was complete; because he had not brought his lips to breasts, he was called Achilles. He himself also represents the prime of life. If that prime desires Desire—Polyxena—who is alien and foreign to truth, it is killed by a serpent’s venom in an arrow to the heel, as death creeps in along the footprint.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"τὸ δεῖπνον ἐτέλει Ζεὺς ὑπέρ τε τῆς Νηρηΐδος Θέτιδος καὶ τοῦ καλοῦ Πηλέως","chosen":"Zeus was holding the feast for the Nereid Thetis and the beautiful Peleus","rationale":"τελεῖν a feast means to conduct or celebrate it; ὑπέρ identifies those for whom or in whose honor it is held."},{"source_quote":"τὰ οὐράνια τῶν Μοιρῶν περιστηρίγματα","chosen":"the Fates’ heavenly encircling supports","rationale":"περιστηρίγματα is rare and denotes structures set or supporting something around a circumference; “surrounding fixtures” is another possible rendering."},{"source_quote":"Προμηθεὺς ἡ προμήθεια","chosen":"Prometheus is forethought","rationale":"The translation preserves the explicit etymological wordplay between Προμηθεύς and προμήθεια."},{"source_quote":"Πηλεὺς πηλὸς ὁ ἀπὸ γῆς εἰς ἀνθρώπου γένεσιν περινοηθεὶς","chosen":"Peleus is mud, conceived from earth for the making of a human being","rationale":"πηλός preserves the wordplay with Peleus. περινοηθείς is taken in its mental sense, “conceived” or “devised,” though “selected” is also contextually possible."},{"source_quote":"ὁ πρῶτος οὐ γεννηθεὶς ἀλλὰ πλασθεὶς τέλειος","chosen":"the first human was not begotten but molded, and was complete","rationale":"The masculine ὁ πρῶτος resumes the preceding ἀνθρώπου. τέλειος can mean complete, perfect, mature, or full-grown."},{"source_quote":"διὰ τὸ μαζοῖς χείλη μὴ προσενεγκεῖν Ἀχιλλεὺς προσηγορεύθη","chosen":"because he had not brought his lips to breasts, he was called Achilles","rationale":"The source supplies an allegorical etymology linking Achilles with the absence of nursing at the breast; the explanation is preserved without replacing it with a modern etymology."},{"source_quote":"ἰῷ ὄφεως ἀναιρεῖται βέλει κατὰ πτέρναν καὶ κατὰ ἴχνος ἐνέρποντος τοῦ θανάτου","chosen":"it is killed by a serpent’s venom in an arrow to the heel, as death creeps in along the footprint","rationale":"Both ἰῷ and βέλει may be read instrumentally. The rendering treats the venom as conveyed by the arrow; alternatively, the phrases may be appositional: “by serpent venom—by an arrow at the heel.”"}],"source_issues":[{"source_quote":"ἔστι δὲ αὐτὸς καὶ ἀκμήν, ἥτις","issue":"The printed ἀκμήν is formally accusative or adverbial, whereas the predicate after ἔστι and the feminine nominative relative ἥτις would ordinarily call for ἀκμή. The context nevertheless supports reference to the prime of life, so a defensible translation is possible without silently altering the supplied reading.","proposed_reading":"ἔστι δὲ αὐτὸς καὶ ἀκμή, ἥτις","blocks_publication":false}]},{"reference":"6.15","text":"Hera, then, and Athena and Aphrodite and Eris and the apple and Hermes and the judgment and the shepherd hint at some such meaning: Hera is dignity; Athena, courage; Aphrodite, pleasures; Hermes, interpreting reason; and Paris the shepherd, the unreasoning and barbarous impulse. So if, at the prime of life, the reasoning faculty that shepherds the soul happens to be barbarous and, passing over what is beneficial—thrusting aside both courage and self-control—chooses pleasures alone and awards victory to desire alone, as though receiving delightful things from her in return, then the one who judged wrongly will receive enjoyment to the destruction of both himself and those who are his. Eris is contentious vice. The golden apple of the Hesperides would be wealth, which sometimes knows how to lead even the self-controlled—as Hera—toward idleness, makes the courageous—as Athena—more contentious over things unfitting for them, and, under the pretext of luxury, destroys beauty of soul—as Aphrodite. I will put it briefly: wealth provokes everyone to evil strife.","lexical_decisions":[{"source_quote":"Ἑρμῆς ὁ ἑρμηνευτικὸς λόγος","chosen":"Hermes, interpreting reason","rationale":"λόγος here belongs to the psychological allegory and is therefore rendered “reason”; ἑρμηνευτικός also sustains the wordplay with Hermes. “Interpretive discourse” is possible."},{"source_quote":"ὁ ποιμὴν Πάρις ἡ ἀλόγιστος ὁρμὴ καὶ βάρβαρος","chosen":"Paris the shepherd, the unreasoning and barbarous impulse","rationale":"ὁρμή denotes impulse or drive, while ἀλόγιστος marks it as lacking rational deliberation."},{"source_quote":"ὁ τὴν ψυχὴν ποιμαίνων λογισμὸς","chosen":"the reasoning faculty that shepherds the soul","rationale":"The rendering preserves the shepherd image in ποιμαίνων and distinguishes λογισμός as the faculty of calculation or reasoning."},{"source_quote":"ὡς παρ’ αὐτῆς τὰ τέρποντα ἀντιλαμβάνων","chosen":"as though receiving delightful things from her in return","rationale":"ἀντιλαμβάνων expresses receiving something in exchange or return; ὡς allows the motivation to be presented as the reasoner’s supposition."},{"source_quote":"ἐπ’ ὀλέθρῳ ἑαυτοῦ τε καὶ τῶν αὐτοῦ","chosen":"to the destruction of both himself and those who are his","rationale":"τῶν αὐτοῦ is deliberately broad and may denote his people, household, or possessions; “those who are his” preserves that ambiguity."},{"source_quote":"ἡ φιλονεικοῦσα κακία","chosen":"contentious vice","rationale":"φιλονεικοῦσα characterizes vice as loving disputes or strife."},{"source_quote":"προφάσει τρυφῆς","chosen":"under the pretext of luxury","rationale":"πρόφασις is a pretext or professed ground, while τρυφή denotes luxury, indulgence, or soft living."}],"source_issues":[]}]}
